barber-state-readiness-check-cutting-016.prompt: A nape needs to melt from a #2 into longer hair with no shelf. The barber holds a comb almost parallel to the scalp and runs a clipper across the teeth. What is this clipper-over-comb pass doing?

options.a: Cutting a graduated plane so a #2 melts into longer hair
options.b: Stamping a blocked square neckline a finger above the natural nape
options.c: Carving a disconnected undercut that leaves a hard occipital ledge
options.d: Notching crown ends with shears to add movement through the top

barber-state-readiness-check-cutting-016.explanation: Clipper-over-comb uses the comb as a moving cutting guide. Held nearly parallel to the head, it lets the clipper take a graduated plane so short nape hair blends into longer parietal hair without a weight line. A single guard, a blocked neckline, or shears on the crown do not create that blend.

distractorExplanations.b: A blocked neckline is an outline choice made with trimmers; it is not what clipper-over-comb on a parallel comb is for.
distractorExplanations.c: A disconnected undercut keeps a visible ledge; clipper-over-comb is the opposite — a blend with no shelf.
distractorExplanations.d: Point-cutting or notching with shears textures the top; it does not blend a #2 nape on a comb.

barber-state-readiness-check-cutting-017.prompt: A mid fade shows a dark band between the 0.5 and 1.5. What is the correct next blending move?

options.a: Drop a foil shaver on the band and erase it in one aggressive pass
options.b: Work lever and overlapping guards through the band until it fades
options.c: Chew the dark band out with thinning shears walked down the side
options.d: Raise the guideline an inch so the band hides under a new hard line

barber-state-readiness-check-cutting-017.explanation: A fade is stacked, overlapping lengths. A dark band is leftover density between two guards; open and close the lever and rework that zone with the next overlapping guard until the shadow melts. Skipping to a shaver, thinning shears, or a new hard line does not blend the band — it either nicks, textures the wrong hair, or moves the shelf.

distractorExplanations.a: A foil shaver finishes skin at the very bottom; using it on a 0.5–1.5 band jumps the fade and often nicks.
distractorExplanations.c: Thinning shears remove bulk in longer hair; they do not fade clipper density at the sideburn/temple.
distractorExplanations.d: Raising the guideline just relocates the shelf; the band still has to be faded where it sits.

barber-state-readiness-check-cutting-018.prompt: On a traditional straight-razor shave, why is the first pass taken with the grain rather than against it?

options.a: To finish the beard in one stroke so a second pass is never needed
options.b: To lift each hair so later strokes can cut against the grain immediately
options.c: To shorten stubble safely before any closer against-grain work
options.d: To skip the hot towel, because with-grain cutting already softens hair

barber-state-readiness-check-cutting-018.explanation: With-the-grain is the safer first reduction. It shortens the beard and lowers drag before a closer second pass (across or against the grain) on already-prepared skin. Going against the grain first on long, unreduced stubble raises nick and irritation risk. The hot towel still belongs before any razor pass.

distractorExplanations.a: The first with-grain pass is a reduction, not a complete shave; a closer pass often follows on the same lather sequence.
distractorExplanations.b: Lifting for an immediate against-grain cut is the opposite of the first-pass rule; against-grain is later and lighter.
distractorExplanations.d: A hot towel still softens the beard and skin; stroke direction does not replace preparation.

barber-state-readiness-check-cutting-019.prompt: Cutting a dry textured crop, the barber over-tensions a parietal section between the fingers. What happens when that hair is released?

options.a: The section springs back longer, so the finished length looks fuller
options.b: Curl stretches flat and the cowlick stays down without extra product
options.c: Dry tension matches a wet-cut elevation, so both methods land the same
options.d: Hair past natural fall springs shorter and can leave a hole

barber-state-readiness-check-cutting-019.explanation: Tension pulls hair past its natural fall. Once released, the hair shortens — more so on dry, wavy, or curly hair — so an over-tensioned dry section can sit too short and print as a hole. Control tension so the cutting line matches how the hair will lie; do not stretch a crop as if it were a wet, maximum-tension classic cut.

distractorExplanations.a: Over-tension makes released hair shorter, not longer; fullness comes from leaving length and cutting with less stretch.
distractorExplanations.b: Stretching a cowlick or curl to cut it often makes it stand more once it rebounds; weight and growth direction hold it down.
distractorExplanations.c: Wet hair stretches more than dry hair; matching wet elevation on a dry crop is a common way to overcut.

barber-state-readiness-check-cutting-020.prompt: The crown has two swirl directions. If the barber cuts that area as one uniform downward growth, what is the likely finish?

options.a: A hole or a spike where the second swirl lifts after the cut
options.b: A double crown that lies flat after two weeks of daily product
options.c: Both swirls flattened by a #1, because short hair cannot stand up
options.d: A hard part forming on its own if the hair is combed to one side

barber-state-readiness-check-cutting-020.explanation: Growth pattern, not the comb, decides how hair sits. A double crown has two lift directions; cutting it as one downward plane takes too much from the swirl that stands, so it spikes or leaves a hole. Cut with each swirl, leave a little length at the lift, and avoid forcing one guideline across both directions.

distractorExplanations.b: Product and time do not retrain a growth pattern; a swirl cut too short still stands after two weeks.
distractorExplanations.c: Cutting a swirl very short usually makes it more visible, not flatter — there is no weight left to hold it down.
distractorExplanations.d: A hard part is a cut or shaved line the client asked for; combing a double crown to the side does not create one.

barber-state-readiness-check-cutting-021.prompt: A round-faced client wants a skin fade with weight on top. Which cut most helps the face read longer, not wider?

options.a: Even, bowl-like length that stacks bulk at the widest part of the cheeks
options.b: Height through the top and a tighter side fade to slim the silhouette
options.c: A full unlined cheek beard that rounds the jaw and fills the sides
options.d: Heavy brow-length bangs that shorten the forehead and fill the face

barber-state-readiness-check-cutting-021.explanation: Face-shape design for a round face adds vertical height and keeps the sides close so the head reads oval, not spherical. A skin or tight fade with length and lift on top does that. Width at the cheeks, a round unlined beard, or heavy bangs all add horizontal bulk and make the face look rounder.

distractorExplanations.a: A bowl or even-length stack sits at the widest part of a round face and emphasizes width.
distractorExplanations.c: An unlined full cheek beard adds side bulk; a higher cheek line and more jaw can slim, but filling the sides does not.
distractorExplanations.d: Bangs that shorten the forehead reduce vertical length — the opposite of what a round face usually needs.

barber-state-readiness-check-cutting-022.prompt: The client wants about three inches left on top with a soft perimeter, and a tight fade on the sides. Which tool split is correct?

options.a: A #8 guard over the whole top, because numbered guards replace shears
options.b: A foil shaver across the crown to polish that three-inch length evenly
options.c: Clipper-over-comb on top with a 000 blade to take bulk only, not length
options.d: Shears or shear-over-comb on top; clippers and shaver stay on the sides

barber-state-readiness-check-cutting-022.explanation: Clippers and guards excel at short, even, or faded lengths on the sides and nape. Three inches of top hair with a soft perimeter is shear or shear-over-comb work: fingers or a comb set the line, and the clipper would either leave a hat line or take too much. Keep the foil shaver and short blades on the fade, not on the crown.

distractorExplanations.a: Even a high guard is still a clipper plane; it will not leave a true three-inch, finger-shaped top the way shears will.
distractorExplanations.b: A foil shaver is for skin and bald-fade finish; it has no business on three-inch crown hair.
distractorExplanations.c: A 000 blade on top would scalp or disconnect; clipper-over-comb at that blade length is a fade tool, not a long-top tool.

barber-state-readiness-check-cutting-023.prompt: A strong frontal cowlick keeps kicking up after a tight crop. What correction respects the growth instead of fighting it?

options.a: Leave extra length and cut with the growth so weight holds it down
options.b: Cut the cowlick to the scalp so there is no hair left that can stand
options.c: Thin the cowlick heavily so fewer hairs remain to lift at the hairline
options.d: Cut against the growth to train the cowlick to reverse its direction

barber-state-readiness-check-cutting-023.explanation: A cowlick is a growth pattern, not a styling error. Leaving a little extra length and cutting with the swirl gives the hair weight so it can lie. Scalping, heavy thinning, or cutting against the growth removes that weight or springs the hair up, so the kick gets worse as it grows.

distractorExplanations.b: Ultra-short cowlicks stand more, not less; there is no length left to weigh the swirl down.
distractorExplanations.c: Thinning removes the interior weight that helps a cowlick lie; the remaining hairs still lift.
distractorExplanations.d: Hair cannot be retrained by cutting against the grain; it rebounds and often leaves a hole.

barber-state-readiness-check-cutting-024.prompt: While clipper-over-combing the parietal ridge, the comb tips far off the head instead of staying on the cutting plane. What usually shows in the finish?

options.a: A cleaner skin-to-#3 fade, because a steep comb increases the blend
options.b: A tighter nape, because the comb compresses hair against the skull
options.c: A shelf or hole where the clipper jumps off the intended plane
options.d: Softer texture, because a steep comb mimics thinning-shear teeth

barber-state-readiness-check-cutting-024.explanation: In clipper-over-comb the comb is the cutting plane. If the teeth angle sharply away from the head, the clipper takes more (or less) than the intended graduation and a weight line or hole appears at that jump. Keep the comb on a consistent plane and move it in small, overlapping bites — steep tipping is not a texture or fade trick.

distractorExplanations.a: A steep comb breaks the plane; it does not improve a skin-to-#3 blend.
distractorExplanations.b: Parietal-ridge angle does not tighten the nape; nape length is a separate, lower zone.
distractorExplanations.d: Texture from thinning shears is a different tool and a different hair length; comb angle is not a thinning substitute.

barber-state-readiness-check-cutting-025.prompt: A low taper should disappear into the natural hairline, but a dark shadow sits at the occipital. What usually caused that line?

options.a: Too many overlapping guards, which over-blend and print as a shadow
options.b: A leftover guideline step that was never faded with the lever
options.c: Shear-over-comb on top pushing a dark band down into the nape
options.d: Following the natural hairline, which always reads as a fade line

barber-state-readiness-check-cutting-025.explanation: Tapers fail at the guideline. If the first clipper track is left as a step, that density prints as a shadow at the occipital until you open the lever and work overlapping lengths through it. Over-blending, top shears, and the natural hairline itself are not what create that band — an unfaded step is.

distractorExplanations.a: Overlapping guards are how you remove a shadow; too little overlap, not too much, leaves the line.
distractorExplanations.c: Shear-over-comb on top does not deposit a clipper guideline at the nape.
distractorExplanations.d: A natural hairline is the taper's destination; following it is not the same as leaving a clipper step.

barber-state-readiness-check-cutting-026.prompt: On a cheek pass with a straight razor, the teaching angle is about 30 degrees to the skin. If the blade lies almost flat and the barber presses to make it cut, what is the risk?

options.a: A closer first with-grain pass that can replace lather on that cheek
options.b: Correct against-grain work, because a flat edge must scoop the follicle
options.c: No cut at all, because a flat razor cannot injure living skin
options.d: Skipping and scraping, so extra pressure becomes nicks and burn

barber-state-readiness-check-cutting-026.explanation: A straight razor cuts cleanly near 30 degrees. Too flat and the edge skips or scrapes; the barber then adds pressure and nicks or burns the cheek. Too steep and the point digs. Keep a light, consistent 30-degree lie with stretching fingers — do not flatten the blade and lean on it to compensate.

distractorExplanations.a: Lather and a proper angle still matter; a flat, pressed blade does not complete a with-grain pass more safely.
distractorExplanations.b: Against-grain work still uses a controlled angle and light pressure, not a scooped flat blade.
distractorExplanations.c: A flat razor still cuts when pressed; skipping plus pressure is a common nick pattern, not a safety feature.

barber-state-readiness-check-cutting-027.prompt: After a scissor crop, the barber cross-checks the top. What is that actually checking?

options.a: The same hair from the opposite angle, looking for holes
options.b: Every section recut at the original elevation and finger angle
options.c: Today's guard numbers against the ticket from the last visit
options.d: The reference photo beside the mirror to confirm the style name

barber-state-readiness-check-cutting-027.explanation: Cross-checking is quality control: comb and cut from a different (often opposite) direction so holes, long corners, and uneven graduation show. Recutting the same way repeats the error. Guard history and photos are consultation, not a geometric check of the finished shape.

distractorExplanations.b: Repeating the original elevation hides the same mistakes; the point is a new angle, not a second identical pass.
distractorExplanations.c: Matching last visit's guards is consultation and record-keeping, not cross-checking the crop.
distractorExplanations.d: A photo checks style agreement; it does not reveal a hole in the interior graduation.

barber-state-readiness-check-cutting-028.prompt: Length on a dense top is already correct, but the shape is too bulky. How should thinning shears be used?

options.a: Walk them down the blunt nape line to fade the perimeter into skin
options.b: Take interior bulk mid-shaft and leave the outline and ends intact
options.c: Replace the clipper at the temples for a skin-tight bald fade
options.d: Drop the whole top to the new length in one pass, since they remove all hair

barber-state-readiness-check-cutting-028.explanation: Thinning shears remove a fraction of the hair per bite. Used mid-shaft in the interior, they drop bulk without shortening the outline or chewing the ends into wisps. They are not a fade tool, a nape-liner, or a replacement for cutting shears when true length still needs to come off.

distractorExplanations.a: A blunt nape and a fade are clipper/trimmer work; thinning shears on the perimeter eat the outline.
distractorExplanations.c: Bald-fade temples are clipper and shaver work; thinning shears cannot take hair to skin evenly.
distractorExplanations.d: Each bite removes only some hairs; they will not drop overall length the way cutting shears do.

barber-state-readiness-check-cutting-029.prompt: A client with a receding nape wants a neckline that will not print as a dark shelf five days later. Which finish is the better professional choice?

options.a: A high blocked square cut well above the natural hairline
options.b: A razor-shaved inverted-V carved into the natural nape growth
options.c: A tapered neckline that follows natural growth so regrowth stays soft
options.d: The shop's standard blocked line, used on every client for consistency

barber-state-readiness-check-cutting-029.explanation: A tapered neckline follows the natural hairline and fades the edge, so five-day growth still looks like a blend instead of a dark block. A high square or inverted-V cut above the natural growth creates a hard shelf as soon as hair returns. Style still follows the consultation, but for a receding nape that must grow out clean, taper beats a high block.

distractorExplanations.a: A high block above the natural line is exactly what grows in as a dark shelf within days.
distractorExplanations.b: An inverted-V shaved into natural growth is a graphic outline; it grows in as a mark, not a soft taper.
distractorExplanations.d: One blocked recipe ignores hairline and grow-out; neckline shape is a client-and-growth decision.

barber-state-readiness-check-cutting-030.prompt: When blending a beard into a cheek skin fade, the join should not leave a dark shelf. Where should the cheek line sit?

options.a: At the highest natural cheek growth so the beard reads as full as possible
options.b: On last week's line from another client who had similar beard density
options.c: On the barber's signature cheek shape, independent of this client's jaw
options.d: On this client's bone structure and the line agreed in the chair

barber-state-readiness-check-cutting-030.explanation: Beard-to-fade work is design plus blend. The cheek line follows the client's bone (zygomatic and jaw) and the line they approved; then overlapping clipper lengths melt beard density into the fade so no shelf sits at the join. Copying another client's line, maxing fullness at the highest growth, or imposing a shop signature all ignore this face and usually leave a step.

distractorExplanations.a: Highest natural growth often sits too far up the cheek and fights the fade; fullness is not the same as a clean join.
distractorExplanations.b: Another client's line will not match this zygomatic and jaw; density alone is not a template.
distractorExplanations.c: A signature shape that ignores the jaw is the barber designing for himself, not for the fade or the client.
